reported.title: Unauthenticated RCE via host param in /lookup (shell command injection)
reported.description: Entry: src/server.js:15 (the GET /lookup handler reads url.searchParams.get('host') and passes it straight to lookupHost). Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the boundary from an untrusted HTTP request into arbitrary OS command execution as the user running the server. The path is: line 12 parses req.url, line 13 only checks the pathname, line 15 reads the caller-controlled host parameter, line 6 forwards it to lookupHost, and line 7 concatenates it into 'getent hosts ' + host before passing the string to child_process.exec, which always runs the string through a shell (/bin/sh -c). Nothing on the path stops it: a repo-wide search finds no authentication, authorization, session, role, guard or middleware code at all, host is never validated, escaped or checked against an allow-list, URL query decoding leaves shell metacharacters such as ;, |, &&, $(), backticks and newlines intact, the '|| localhost' fallback only replaces missing or empty values, and exec (unlike execFile or spawn without a shell) invokes a shell by design. A request such as /lookup?host=;id or /lookup?host=$(cat%20/etc/passwd) executes arbitrary commands, and lines 16-17 return the command stdout inside the JSON body, so the attacker reads the output directly. Impact: unauthenticated remote code execution on the server host, enabling file and credential theft, access to internal networks, and full machine compromise. Fix: replace exec with execFile('getent', ['hosts', host]) so no shell is involved, validate host against a strict hostname/IP allow-list, and require authentication plus an authorization check before the lookup runs (or bind the listener to loopback).

reported.title: Unauthenticated /lookup endpoint lets any network caller drive server-side host lookups
reported.description:
Entry: src/server.js:14
Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller who can reach the listening port, crossing the authentication/authorization boundary of the service's privileged server-side lookup operation — the handler runs a host-resolution command for anyone who connects, with no credential, role, tenant or ownership check anywhere in the code.
Path: GET /lookup?host=<value> reaches the createServer callback (src/server.js:12); line 14 only compares url.pathname to '/lookup'; line 16 reads the caller-controlled host parameter (defaulting to 'localhost' when absent) and passes it directly to lookupHost; lookupHost applies only the character-class regex at line 7 and then executes execAsync('getent', ['hosts', host]) at line 8, returning the command's stdout to the caller at lines 17-18.
Why nothing on the path stops it: the service contains no authentication or authorization logic at all — no token/cookie/header check, no caller allow-list, no role or ownership check — and the only rejection branch (404) applies to paths other than /lookup. The regex at line 7 validates the shape of the string, not who sent it, and the server is started with listen(Number(process.env.PORT || 3000)) at line 23 without a bind address, so Node listens on all interfaces and the unauthenticated endpoint is reachable from the network by default; there is also no rate limit constraining the caller.
Impact for this application: any unauthenticated network user can drive the server's own host/DNS resolution as a proxy — enumerate internal hostnames that resolve from the server's network position, read back the resolved addresses (and the server's hosts database), force DNS traffic to originate from the server (blind SSRF), and spawn one getent process per request (2s timeout, no throttling) for a cheap denial of service against the service host.
Fix: require authentication and authorization before handling /lookup (reject requests without a valid credential prior to reading host), bind the listener to loopback or a protected interface if the endpoint is internal-only, and reject host values with a leading '-' so the value cannot be interpreted as a getent option.

reported.title: Option injection in getent lookup leaks /etc/hosts to unauthenticated clients
reported.description:
Entry: src/server.js:16 (handler at src/server.js:12-14; the only route is GET /lookup?host=..., and there is no authentication or authorization check anywhere in the file).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network client that can reach the port (createLookupServer().listen(...) at line 23 binds all interfaces), crossing the boundary that the caller's value is a hostname to be looked up rather than an option for the program the server spawns.
Path: line 13 parses req.url, line 16 takes url.searchParams.get('host'), line 7 is the only validation (/^[a-zA-Z0-9._:-]{1,253}$/), and line 8 hands the value straight into the child process argv: execAsync('getent', ['hosts', host], ...).
Why nothing stops it: the allow-list still permits a value that begins with '-' (the hyphen is the final member of the character class, so it is literal and legal in any position), and the argv contains no '--' terminator, so getent's getopt_long parses the caller's value as an option instead of the lookup key. ?host=-- ends option parsing and leaves no key, so glibc's getent enumerates the entire hosts database (sethostent/gethostent loop) and line 18 returns every entry of the server's /etc/hosts, i.e. internal hostnames and their IP addresses, to the caller; ?host=--help, ?host=--version, ?host=-4, ?host=-6, ?host=-i, ?host=-w and ?host=-a are likewise consumed as options and change the mode of the invoked tool. No shell is involved, so shell metacharacters are irrelevant here, but nothing rejects a leading hyphen, no '--' is inserted, and the route requires no credentials.
Impact: an outsider with no account obtains server-local host data (the hosts table, i.e. an internal name-to-address map) and can force the lookup tool into modes it was never meant to expose, which is direct internal-network reconnaissance from the server's own network position; the same value also drives the server's resolver, so internal-only names resolve from inside and their addresses come back.
Fix: pass the terminator and constrain the first character, e.g. execAsync('getent', ['hosts', '--', host], ...) together with a check such as /^(?![.-])[a-zA-Z0-9._:-]{1,253}$/, and preferably drop the subprocess entirely in favour of dns.lookup/net.isIP so no option parsing can occur.
